Learn Arabic letters and short vowels
Recognize each letter and its vocalization marks. Practice reading single-letter syllables.
Practice the basic Arabic letters: اَ بَ تَ ثَ جَ حَ خَ دَ ذَ رَ زَ سَ شَ صَ ضَ طَ ظَ عَ غَ فَ قَ كَ لَ مَ نَ وَ هَ يَ. Focus on clear pronunciation of each letter with the short \"a\" vowel (Fatha).
Study maddah lengthening and the sukun sign. Read simple words with short and long vowels.
Learn long vowels (Maddah) like بَا, تَا, ثَا and the silent sign (Sukun) like أَبْ, أَتْ, أَجْ. Sukun indicates that the letter is pronounced without any vowel sound.
Read nun sukun, tanwin, and mim sukun
Practice rules for nun and mim reading. See how sounds change before different letters.
Learn the double vowel markings (Tanwin) which sound like \"an\", \"in\", \"un\" (e.g., بً, تٍ, ثٌ). Practice reading nun sukun and mim sukun with clear, distinct pronunciation.
Study idgham, iqlab, and ikhfa. Read examples without audio to build visual rule recognition.

Learn the rules of merging and changing sounds: Idgham (blending sounds together, e.g., مَنْ يَقُولُ becomes may-yaqul) and Iqlab (changing the sound of Nun to Mim, e.g., مِنْ بَعْدِ becomes mim-ba\'d).
Practice bouncing consonants at the end
Recognize qalqalah stops in words. Focus on the shape and letter sequence rather than sound.
Qalqalah triggers a slight bounce on letters ق ط ب ج د when they stop. Practice ending words like أَقْتَبَ.
Read short combinations: بَسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ, أَلْمُ, نُونٌ، مِيمٌ. Focus on letter shape and vowel marking.
Read short Arabic combinations and words. This lesson reinforces the previous rules in context.

Qiyam is voluntary night prayer — often called tahajud when prayed after sleep.
The last third of the night is a blessed time for dua and extra rakah. Log here when you stand for qiyam tonight.
Expand each section for Arabic text, transliteration, and step-by-step guidance for tahajud / qiyam.
Best time — last third of night
Sleep with intention to wake for tahajud. The last third of the night (between Isha and Fajr) is especially blessed. Even two rakah before Fajr count as tahajud.
Make intention in your heart before takbir. Example: I intend to pray sunnah tahajud for Allah.
نَوَيْتُ أَنْ أُصَلِّيَ سُنَّةَ التَّهَجُّدِ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى
Nawaytu an usalliya sunnata at-tahajjudi lillāhi taʿālā
Raise hands and say Allahu Akbar to begin each rakah pair. Face the qibla with wudu.
After takbir, you may recite the opening dua before Al-Fatihah in the first rakah.
سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ، وَتَبَارَكَ اسْمُكَ، وَتَعَالَى جَدُّكَ، وَلَا إِلَٰهَ غَيْرُكَ
Subḥānaka Allāhumma wa biḥamdika, wa tabāraka smuka, wa taʿālā jadduka, wa lā ilāha ghayruk
Recite Al-Fatihah in every rakah, then a short surah or a few verses in the first two rakah of each pair.
Common choices: Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, An-Nas, Al-Kafirun, or any surah you know. Tahajud is prayed in pairs of two rakah — say salam after every two.
Bow with back straight, hands on knees. Say tasbih at least 3 times.
Prostrate with forehead, nose, hands, knees, and toes on the ground. Say tasbih at least 3 times per sajdah.
End the night with witr — minimum 1 rakah, commonly 3. In the final rakah, raise hands for qunut before ruku (per your madhab). After witr, do not pray more sunnah.
Recite qunut in the last rakah of witr while standing, before ruku. Many scholars allow a shorter dua if the full text is difficult to memorize.
اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِنِي فِيمَنْ هَدَيْتَ، وَعَافِنِي فِيمَنْ عَافَيْتَ، وَتَوَلَّنِي فِيمَنْ تَوَلَّيْتَ، وَبَارِكْ لِي فِيمَا أَعْطَيْتَ

The last third of the night is when Allah descends (in a manner befitting Him) and answers dua. Ask for forgiveness, guidance, family, and the ummah. Speak from the heart in any language.

Hajb, ashab al-furud, asabah, awl & radd

Faraidh is the Islamic science of inheritance distribution after death. This tool calculates each heir\'s Quranic share (furud), residue (asabah), blocking rules (hajb), and special adjustments (ʿawl when shares exceed the estate, radd when surplus remains). Use it for planning and education—always consult a qualified scholar for binding legal rulings.
The case posed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (RA) while on the minbar: shares exceed 1 so ʿawl applies — the wife receives ¼ of her normal entitlement.

The muddled case: grandfather and full sister each receive 1/6 fixed, then pool and redivide their combined 2/6 in a 2:1 ratio (grandfather 2 parts, sister 1 part) — Ibn Masʿūd and Zayd ibn Thābit ruling.
Al-Mushtaraka: ʿUmar ibn Al-Khaṭṭāb (RA) ruled that full brothers share equally with maternal siblings in the 1/3 — applied in the Mālikī madhhab.
The two ʿUmari rulings: when both parents and a spouse survive with no children, the mother receives 1/3 of the residue (after the spouse\'s share) — not 1/3 of the whole estate.
ʿAwl applied — shares scaled proportionally because fixed portions exceeded the estate.
Radd applied — surplus redistributed among blood heirs (spouses excluded).

A collection of selected verses for protection from sihr, jinn, and harm, compiled by scholars in the Indian subcontinent.
Begin Manzil with Al-Fatihah — the greatest surah, recited in every rakah. A cure and protection.
Continue with the opening of Al-Baqarah — guidance for the God-conscious and the path to success.
Your God is One — there is no deity but Him, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
The greatest verse in the Quran — a fortress of protection. Whoever recites it at night remains under Allah\'s protection until morning.
There is no compulsion in religion — truth has become clear from falsehood.
Allah is the Protector of the believers, bringing them from darkness into light.
To Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and earth — He will call you to account for what is in your hearts.
The Messenger and believers have faith in what was revealed — we hear and we obey, seeking Your forgiveness.
Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity — the closing supplication of Al-Baqarah for forgiveness and help.
Allah testifies that there is no deity but Him — the Almighty, the All-Wise.
Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty — You give honour and power to whom You will.
You cause the night to enter the day and bring the living from the dead — You provide for whom You will without measure.
Your Lord created the heavens and earth in six days — call upon Him humbly and in secret.
Call upon Allah or Ar-Rahman — to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names. Praise be to Him who has no son nor partner.
Were you created without purpose? Exalted is Allah, the True King — seek His forgiveness and mercy.
By the angels ranged in rows — your God is One, Lord of the heavens and the earth.
O assembly of jinn and men — none can escape Allah\'s authority. Which of your Lord\'s favours will you deny?
If this Quran were sent upon a mountain, it would crumble — He is Allah, the Creator, the Bestower of Forms, the Most Beautiful Names.
A group of jinn heard the Quran, believed, and declared their faith — our Lord has no spouse or child.
A declaration of disavowal from disbelief — to you your religion, to me mine.
The essence of Tawheed — He is Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who begets not nor is begotten.
Seek refuge with the Lord of daybreak from the evil of creation, darkness, sorcery, and envy.
Seek refuge with the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind, from the whisperer who withdraws.

Manzil (Arabic: منزل) is a system for dividing the recitation of the Quran to facilitate completing (khatam) the Quran over seven days (one week). This tradition is widely practiced in South Asian Muslim communities and has been popularized by scholars such as Shah Waliullah al-Dehlawi.\n\nNote: "Manzil" here refers to the 7-part Quran division for khatam, and is different from the protection verses (Manzil ruqyah) compiled by Maulana Zakariyya Kandhlawi. This section in the app covers the protection verses.

A mnemonic phrase meaning "My mouth longs to recite (the Quran)". The 7 letters — ف م ي ب ش و ق — are the first letters of the surah that begins each of the 7 Manzils: Al-Fatihah, Al-Ma\'idah, Yunus, Al-Isra\', Asy-Syu\'ara, Ash-Shaffat, and Qaf.

Each day, recite one Manzil in sequence from Monday to Sunday, completing the entire Quran in one week. You may recite it in one sitting or spread it across multiple sessions during the day (e.g. after Fajr, Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isya\').\n\nTo begin, start with Manzil 1 (Juz 1–6) and proceed to the next Manzil each day. Consistency is key — even if you cannot complete a full Manzil in a day, try to at least read a portion and continue the next day.

Enables regular completion (khatam) of the Quran — once per week.|Builds a strong, consistent relationship with the Book of Allah.|Reciting the entire Quran regularly earns great reward and forgiveness.|Encourages daily reflection on different parts of the Quran.|A structured approach recommended by classical scholars and passed down through generations.

SĀAT is a modern, comprehensive companion application designed to elevate your daily Islamic routines.
